title: Breaking and Entering: Fever Ray
summary: Simon and Lauren are joined on the line for a special interview with Swedish music royalty - producer & songwriter Karin Dreijer aka Fever Ray.
transcript:
Karin Dreijer, who records as Fever Ray, joined Lauren Taylor and Simon Winkler remotely for this Breaking and Entering interview, broadcast on 9 May 2024. Their third Fever Ray album, Radical Romantics, released in March 2023 and featured as a Triple R Album of the Week, explored love and included contributions from their sibling Olof Dreijer. The conversation begins with bell hooks' All About Love and its idea of love as an action, before turning to music, intuition and working with Olof.

Karin: I think definitely, because overall I think feelings are something that I have struggled with forever. I don't remember who gave me that book, but I think when I started to read it, it took a lot of time. I think I've read it like hundreds of times, because first you read it and you start to think about it, but then to put your thoughts into action and start changing a behaviour, that is the tricky, tricky thing. It takes a lot of practice and time. So I think it's been an ongoing shift, and also it's still an ongoing shift, because in every relationship you start to do it in a different way than you've been taught.

Host: We love hearing you talk about that idea of love as a practice, something, as you say, that is a continuing education. You can read it many, many times and continue to practise it. We were curious as to how the new album Radical Romantics might be a reflection or an embodiment of some of your new understandings of what love is and can be.

Karin: I think every time I make music, it's sort of a research of how to have feelings and what to do with them, and how to handle feelings and emotions. Around the time when I wrote this album, I was very curious and struggling to find out how to have romantic relationships. How is it even possible? Also, within our community today, in this super capitalist society that we have today, there is so little time for relationships and how to connect. You need a lot of time for communication and just to be there with friends and romantic partners and family. That is today, I think, a struggle. So it's something that I thought about a lot when I was working on this.

[Music]

Simon: I wanted to ask, I know that Lauren and I think about this a lot when we think about your music, and you just used the word research, this idea of your albums as a form of investigation. We were wondering, with Radical Romantics, and maybe if you wanted to connect it to some of your other albums as well, what it is that you have learned about yourself through the making of this album, and maybe just to address that idea of self-knowledge as well in relation to Radical Romantics.

Karin: I think I've learned that I am impatient. I struggle with patience, and that's a good knowledge. Also, to work against your feelings sometimes is really good. I think this idea of always trusting your gut feeling, that does not work on me, and a lot of people. Because my gut feeling can be like, 'I will run away. I will break up. I will cut my leg off,' or something. Before, when I was scared before doing shows, I was like, 'I'm running away now. I'm just leaving.' Instead of doing those initial thoughts you get, to do the opposite, like, 'I am going to stay here. I'm going to do this, even if I'm frightened.' I'm not 100% good at it, but it's something I practise.

Karin: You can get an idea in a lot of therapy that you will fix something, like, 'If I read this book, I will fix this. If I go to the gym, I will look better.' But I think I've learned it's more like an ongoing process all the time, everything. I know I have to practise doing the things that I'm afraid of, otherwise the fear will come back. You're never fixed.

Host: That's a useful piece of knowledge as well, the idea that everything is a practice, and sitting with that discomfort and learning to be patient with yourself.

Karin: They are so difficult. They are.

[Music]

Host: You were talking before about feelings and emotions being really important for you to explore. You said that music should not be thought about so much, it should come from the body. How do you tap into your intuition and emotions when you're creating music?

Karin: I think it's sort of the only thing for me that comes direct, because music has been an outlet for me, for emotions and to be with myself and to feel things. That is sort of the only time I can trust my gut feeling. It has always been a natural output. Before I started to play instruments myself, I listened to music all the time, and I still listen a lot. For me, music is the best way to be in myself and to feel things. It's a great help to feel different things.

Karin: When you've been away from music, when I tour, from time to time I don't listen to so much music because I have sound in my ears all the time. But now, for example, I have said yes to do a couple of DJ gigs, and I haven't done it for like eight years or something, or maybe five. That's so great, I think, to start listening to just everything and find out what you really feel for. What is it that I think is fun to play today? So I'm very excited about that.

[Music]

Host: This album Radical Romantics was a chance for you to reconnect with your brother as well, Olof. Could you tell us a little bit about that unique relationship and how it is expressed musically?

Karin: It is strange. I started to work with him when he was only like 17, and before that we didn't know each other so well, because I'm six years older and I moved out very early. So he was just a kid and I thought he was very annoying. It is a special kind of relationship. Sometimes it's very much about our work only, so we don't hang out outside of that. But now we have our studios next to each other in a space here. We both travel a lot, but that's where we meet, in the studio space.

Karin: It was great working with him on these tracks. I had no expectations. I didn't know if he wanted to, but it was the pandemic and he was there and I was there. So I was just like, 'Should we just try out a few things?' And he was like, 'Yeah.' I mean, we didn't know. It was such a strange time when you don't know, will we ever get out of here? For how long will this, maybe this will be forever? It was a very strange time. It was very peaceful too, no stress, no deadlines. We just made music.

[Music]

Karin: Martin Falck, who I work very close with on the videos, he does all the graphic art around the albums, the two last ones. He's also one of my best friends. It's a struggle, I think, for both of us. When we reach something that is good and balanced, we start to freak out because we have this gene. I'm saying now, I'm just not taking responsibility for that. But it's something like, when we feel something is starting to get normal or boring, we start to freak out a bit and have to tear it all apart in a way.

Karin: That we can blame on a lot of things. We can say we both have ADHD, but I think it's also a problem in society, this individualism that you have been taught, you have the right to always feel great, also within relationships, and everything should just come to you. So I think for us it's always something lurking in the background.

Host: It sounds like you have an incredible creative partnership with Martin. You mentioned you found that there weren't any love songs in the traditional sense on the new record, more songs about what it means to love. Was that your intention or was it something that simply emerged for you?

Karin: I didn't think of it as a love album or something, no. I was more thinking of it like it's an ongoing research, it's what I always do. But it was more Martin who said it's a love album. I think that is an overall theme. I think it is still not a traditional love song, because it's a bit of a lie, because love is a struggle and there is work in relationships. You have to work to have good relationships. It takes time and effort. So I think it is about that.

[Music]

Host: Will you be doing any DJ sets while you're in Melbourne?

Karin: No, I have to practise now for a bit.
